item.title: The Golang4U LLM Bible: Internals of the Intelligent Llama Manager
item.description:
Preface: Why Native llama.cpp is Painful

Running Large Language Models (LLMs) locally using llama.cpp offers incredible privacy and performance. However, deploying it effectively is notoriously difficult. The native experience is raw: compiling binaries manually, dealing with unoptimized package manager downloads, juggling 50GB file transfers, calculating mental VRAM boundaries, and memorizing arcane CLI flags. Get a single context metric wrong, and your GPU violently crashes with an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) panic.

We built an all-in-one Go application—llama_manager.go—to solve this entirely. It is a highly fault-tolerant daemon that dynamically profiles physical hardware, reverse-engineers a model’s memory footprint on the fly, and calculates the exact parameters needed to run engines at absolute peak efficiency.

item.title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention
item.description:
Preface: The “Correct” Code that Crashes

You can write perfect algorithms, but if you deploy them with default settings, you will crash.

  • Default HTTP Server: Vulnerable to Slowloris.
  • Default GC: Vulnerable to OOM Killers.
  • Default DB Driver: Vulnerable to Connection Storms.

This guide is about Runtime Hardening.

Chapter 1: The Slowloris Attack (Timeouts)

The Attack: A hacker opens 1,000 connections to your server. They send: G… wait 10s … E … wait 10s … T … The default Go http.Server has NO Timeout. It will wait forever. Your RAM fills up with open connections. The server hangs.

item.title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models
item.description:
Preface: Where does logic belong?

In architecture, there is a concept called “Anemic Domain Model”. This is when your structs are just data bags:

1

type User struct { Name string }

And all your logic is in Service:

1

func (s *Service) IsAdult(u *User) bool { return u.Age >= 18 }

Golang4U prefers a Rich Domain Model. We put logic on the struct itself when it applies to the entity.

item.title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems
item.description:
Preface: The Vendor Trap

Every startup guide tells you: “Sign up for SendGrid/Mailgun/AWS SES.” Result involved?

  1. Complexity: You need to manage API keys, webhooks, and SDKs.
  2. Cost: They get expensive fast.
  3. Lock-in: Switching from SendGrid to Mailgun requires rewriting code.

In Golang4U, we choose the Standard Library. Go’s net/smtp is battle-hardened. It speaks the raw protocol of the internet. This guide shows how we built a Vendor-Agnostic emailer.

Chapter 1: The SMTP Protocol (Raw & Real)

Sending an email is just a TCP handshake.

item.title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV
item.description:
Preface: The Upload Vulnerability

Accepting user content is necessary but dangerous. A “Profile Picture” upload form is often a backdoor for:

  1. Shell Uploads: Uploading shell.php to execute code.
  2. Malware Distribution: Hosting a standard Windows virus on your domain.
  3. DoS Attacks: Uploading a 50GB file to fill your disk.

In Golang4U, we treat every file as a potential bomb. This guide explains how we defuse them using Streaming and ClamAV.

Chapter 1: The Magic Bytes (Trust Nothing)

First rule: Never trust the file extension. A file named cute_cat.jpg might actually be a .exe. A file named report.pdf might be a shell script.

item.title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines
item.description:
Preface: The 3 Factors of Auth

Authentication is proving you are who you say you are. There are 3 ways to do this:

  1. Something you Know (Knowledge): Password, PIN, Mother’s Maiden Name.
  2. Something you Have (Possession): Phone, YubiKey, RSA Token.
  3. Something you Are (Inherence): Fingerprint, FaceID, Retina.

A Password alone is weak because it can be phished. 2FA (Two-Factor) combines #1 and #2. Even if a hacker phishes your password, they cannot physically steal your phone over the internet.

item.title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing
item.description:
Preface: Why TLS is Not Enough

HTTPS (TLS 1.3) protects data “In Transit.” It prevents the Hacker in the Coffee Shop from reading your password. But it does not protect against:

  1. Malicious Proxies: A corporate proxy (MITM) that terminates TLS.
  2. The Server Itself: If our logs accidentally print req.Body.
  3. Memory Dumps: If the server crashes and dumps RAM.

To fix this, we implement End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) at the Application Layer. The password is encrypted in the browser and only decrypted inside the Service function.

item.title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design
item.description:
Preface: Authentication vs Authorization

First, a distinction.

  • Authentication (AuthN): “Who are you?” (I am User 123).
  • Authorization (AuthZ): “What can you do?” (I can delete posts).

This, guide focuses on AuthN. specifically, how we securely identify a user across stateless HTTP requests.

Chapter 1: The Fall of JWT (JSON Web Tokens)

For a decade, JWT (RFC 7519) was the king. But heavy lies the crown. A JWT is a string: header.payload.signature.

The Design Flaw: Cipher Agility

The header tells the server how to verify the token.

item.title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass
item.description:
Preface: The Zero Trust Mindset

Security is often treated as a feature. “Add a login page, and we’re secure.” This is false. Security is a Process. It is the sum of every line of code that handles input.

In Golang4U, we adopt a Zero Trust mindset.

  1. Trust No IP: Even if it didn’t attack us yesterday, it might attack us today.
  2. Trust No User: Even if they have a valid token, they might be spamming.
  3. Trust No Browser: Even if Chrome says it’s secure, we enforce it with headers.

This guide will walk you through the three rings of defense: Network, Application, and Presentation.

item.title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass
item.description:
Preface: Why Read This?

If you are just starting with Go, you might write everything in main.go. It works for a “Hello World,” but it fails for a production system. If you are an expert, you might argue about “Clean Architecture” vs “Hexagonal” vs “Onion.”

Golang4U adopts a pragmatic, production-ready Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) structure. It is designed to be:

  1. Testable: Every layer can be mocked.
  2. Scalable: New features (like a “Video” post type) don’t break old ones.
  3. Readable: A new developer knows exactly where to put code.

This guide is not a summary. It is a Masterclass. We will read the code together, line by line, layer by layer. By the end, you will understand not just how it works, but why it was built this way.
